flashcards.q: SRP's 'one reason to change' means one what, per Martin's later clarification?
flashcards.a: One actor/stakeholder whose requirements drive changes to the class — not one method or one verb.

flashcards.q: What is the anemic domain model and which principle misapplication causes it?
flashcards.a: Entities reduced to getters/setters with all logic in external *Service classes; caused by applying SRP to entities themselves instead of to actor-driven collaborators.

flashcards.q: At roughly what branch count does an if/elif dispatch justify becoming an OCP strategy pattern?
flashcards.a: Around 5-8 branches, or when a second independent axis of variation appears (e.g. carrier x region) — not before.

flashcards.q: Why does the classic Square-extends-Rectangle example violate LSP?
flashcards.a: Square must keep width=height, so setWidth silently changes height, breaking any caller's postcondition assumption when Rectangle is substituted with Square.

flashcards.q: What is 'interface bloat' and which principle overapplied causes it?
flashcards.a: One interface per method (IReadable, IWritable, IDeletable...) forcing callers to compose many types; caused by over-applying ISP without real divergence among implementers.

flashcards.q: DIP vs dependency injection — what's the distinction?
flashcards.a: DIP is the principle about which direction the compile-time dependency arrow points (both high and low level depend on an abstraction); DI is a runtime mechanism for supplying an implementation. You can follow DIP without a DI framework.

flashcards.q: When is a DI container the wrong call even though DIP is being followed?
flashcards.a: When there's exactly one implementation, no plan for a second, and no test-isolation need a manual fake couldn't satisfy — the container adds indirection cost with no optionality payoff.

flashcards.q: Who coined the term 'SOLID' and roughly when?
flashcards.a: Michael Feathers, around 2004, packaging five principles Robert C. Martin had collected (two from Meyer/Liskov, three of his own).

flashcards.q: What historical pain did OCP and LSP originally respond to?
flashcards.a: Fragile base class syndrome in 1990s deep inheritance hierarchies, where changes to a shared superclass silently broke subclasses.

flashcards.q: Which SOLID principle has the least legitimate 'overapplication' argument, and why?
flashcards.a: LSP — a genuine violation is a correctness bug, not a taste preference; the closest counter-argument is that fixing it correctly inherits ISP's interface-fragmentation cost.

flashcards.q: How do Go and Python largely give you ISP/DIP 'for free' compared to Java/C#?
flashcards.a: Structural typing (Go interfaces, Python typing.Protocol) — any type satisfying a method set implements the interface with no explicit declaration, unlike nominal typing which requires explicit interfaces and usually a DI container.

flashcards.q: Two variables that decide whether to apply SOLID at all to a piece of code?
flashcards.a: Expected lifetime of the code, and whether an axis of change has actually been observed (not imagined).
